Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
I work hard at keeping busy with other things

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

vignette: Tariq was walking through the lower levels of the Meridian Shopping Plaza, holding a bolt of silk against the light, when the first coordinated blast tore through the food court. The shockwave threw him against a steel pillar, and a fine, acrid powder settled over his skin, instantly cooling his damp palms. He remembered the taste of copper and burnt fabric flooding his mouth, sharp and uninvited. The ceiling groaned, concrete dust choking the air. What stayed with him were not whole scenes but jagged fragments: the sudden flash of blue emergency lights, the heavy thud of a downed shutter, the exact forty-two-degree chill of rainwater mixing with the smoke on his collar. He ran because the floor tilted, and when he finally spilled onto the street, the memories did not arrive as a story. They arrived as a present-tense collapse, his lungs seizing around the same taste, his hands trembling with the same phantom weight. In the weeks that followed, Tariq found his workroom at the edge of the design district becoming less a studio and more a containment unit. The event had not ended; it simply waited. When he reached for a spool of thread, a sudden memory would strike without warning, and he would drop to one knee, stomach lurching with a wave of nausea. The taste of that day returned unbidden, metallic and thick, no matter how many times he rinsed his mouth. He stopped wearing his work jackets because the specific temperature of the wool against his shoulders felt too much like the chill on the plaza floor. He did not try to map the memories, because they did not fit together. They were just fragments pressing against the present, refusing to acknowledge that years had passed. To keep the fragments from breaking through, Tariq learned to fill the hours. He ordered more fabric than he needed, pinned garments to half-finished mannequins, and stayed past midnight running calico through the cutting table. He worked hard at keeping busy. The studio doors and windows demanded constant attention, and he checked them repeatedly until his knuckles ached. He began marking his exits the moment he entered any new space, tracing sightlines to side doors and stairwells before he allowed himself to sit. He had come to believe that comfort was impossible without a way out, so he walked into every room looking for the door. When the pressure built in his chest, heavy and suffocating, he would press a razor blade into the heel of his hand, using the sharp, clean sting to push the overwhelming feelings back down. The habits had taken root over months, and the cost showed in his patterns. Clients noticed that Tariq rarely met them in his main consultation room, preferring to work at a table near the fire exit. He could feel his concentration fraying during fittings. Threads would tangle in his fingers while his eyes kept drifting to the ceiling corners, scanning for the shadows that might signal another collapse. His marriage had dissolved two years earlier, not from a single fracture but from the slow erosion of a man who could no longer sit through a meal without calculating the distance to the street. Now, at forty-eight, Tariq came to therapy because the busyness was no longer enough to quiet the sudden memories. He is most afraid of losing control of his own mind in the middle of a pattern, of the taste returning when he cannot work it away. He hopes to find a way to sit in a room and simply be there, to let the past stay in the past, even when his body remembers what his mind has tried to outrun.
